fields.definition: An audible transient produced when a synthesizer oscillator's waveform makes a sudden step discontinuity, most often when its phase is reset to a fixed start point at note-on or at each hard-sync retrigger. The abrupt jump in the signal carries broadband energy that is heard as a click.
fields.plain_english: A small click you hear when a synth's wave suddenly jumps instead of starting smoothly. It is like the pop you hear if you yank a rope tight all at once instead of pulling it gently.
fields.purpose_function: It is usually an unwanted artifact rather than a feature, so knowing its cause lets a technician choose free-running phase, zero-crossing starts, or anti-click smoothing to keep note attacks clean. A subtle click is sometimes kept on purpose to sharpen a percussive attack.
fields.practical_application: When a bass patch clicks on every note, a technician turns off the oscillator's phase reset (free-run) or enables the synth's click-removal option to clean up the attack.
common_mistakes: Assuming the click means broken gear when it is a normal phase-reset artifact.
Confusing an oscillator click with digital aliasing or a DC-offset thump.
Turning on phase reset for tighter attacks without realizing it can add clicks.
scenario_contexts: A plucky bass patch clicks on every note because the oscillator resets its phase at each note-on.
A hard-synced lead shows small clicks at high sync ratios from the abrupt waveform resets.
Switching an oscillator from reset to free-run to remove clicks from held chords.

sources: Sound on Sound - Synth Secrets series (oscillator waveforms and discontinuities)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (synthesis and oscillators)

fields.definition: A synthesis technique in which one oscillator (the slave) has its waveform cycle forcibly restarted by another oscillator (the master). In hard sync the slave's phase is reset every master cycle, locking its perceived pitch to the master while the slave's own tuning reshapes the waveform into bright, harmonically rich tones; soft sync resets the slave only under certain conditions for a subtler effect.
fields.plain_english: One oscillator forces a second one to restart its wave in step with it. Then you sweep the second one's tuning to get that screaming, tearing lead sound.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to create complex, animated harmonics that a single oscillator cannot make, especially the classic aggressive sync-lead sound when the slave's pitch is swept.
fields.practical_application: A technician sets oscillator 1 as master and oscillator 2 as slave, then modulates oscillator 2's pitch with an envelope to get the tearing sync-lead timbre.
common_mistakes: Thinking hard sync raises the pitch; the master sets the pitch and the slave's tuning shapes the tone.
Not modulating the slave oscillator's tuning and then wondering why sync sounds static.
Confusing hard sync with FM; both add harmonics but by different mechanisms.
scenario_contexts: Programming an aggressive sync-lead by sweeping the slave oscillator with an envelope.
Using soft sync to loosely lock two oscillators for a thicker unison.
Recreating classic 1980s sync tones on a hardware or software synth.

sources: Sound on Sound - Synth Secrets, Part 43 (Oscillator Sync)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (synthesis and oscillators)

fields.definition: Prompt-based sound design is the practice of creating or shaping sounds by writing natural-language text prompts (optionally with reference audio) that drive a generative AI model, rather than by manually programming synthesizer or sampler parameters.
fields.plain_english: It means making sounds by describing them in words. You type something like a rusty metal door creak and the AI makes that sound for you.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a creator specify a target sound in plain language and get usable audio fast, lowering the skill barrier and speeding up sketching or prototyping of sound effects and textures.
fields.practical_application: A sound designer types a prompt such as distant thunder with light rain into a text-to-audio tool, auditions several takes, and drops the best result into the timeline for cleanup.
common_mistakes: Expecting one prompt to nail the sound instead of iterating and refining the wording
Ignoring sample rate, length, and quality limits of the generated output
Assuming generated sounds are automatically license-cleared for release
scenario_contexts: Sketching placeholder SFX before a formal Foley session
Generating ambient textures for a game prototype
Creating quick sound variations from a written description

sources: Stability AI - Stable Audio documentation (text-to-audio / text-to-SFX)
Liu et al., AudioLDM: Text-to-Audio Generation with Latent Diffusion Models (2023)
ElevenLabs - Text to Sound Effects documentation (elevenlabs.io/docs)

fields.definition: RAVE (Realtime Audio Variational autoEncoder) is a neural audio-synthesis model introduced by Caillon and Esling at IRCAM in 2021 that learns a compact latent representation of audio and decodes it back to a waveform, enabling fast, high-quality timbre transfer and generation that can run in real time, even on CPU.
fields.plain_english: RAVE is an AI that learns the sound of an instrument or voice and lets you play or transform audio through it in real time. It is fast enough to run live.
fields.purpose_function: It provides a lightweight neural model for real-time timbre transfer and sound generation, letting musicians route live audio through a trained model to reshape its timbre on stage or in the studio.
fields.practical_application: A musician trains a RAVE model on a chosen sound set, then runs it as a plug-in (for example via nn~ in Max/MSP or Pure Data) to morph a live instrument into that timbre during performance.
common_mistakes: Assuming RAVE needs a huge dataset - it can train on a few hours, but too little varied audio yields artifacts
Confusing RAVE's real-time timbre transfer with text-to-music generation
Expecting perfect fidelity at very low latency without tuning the model size
scenario_contexts: Real-time timbre transfer of a live vocal on stage
Building a custom instrument from a trained sound model in Max/MSP
Generating evolving textures for sound design

sources: Caillon & Esling, RAVE: A variational autoencoder for fast and high-quality neural audio synthesis (arXiv:2111.05011, 2021)
IRCAM ACIDS - official RAVE implementation and documentation (github.com/acids-ircam/RAVE)

fields.definition: A quantization method that encodes a vector with a cascade of vector quantizers, where each stage stores the residual (the leftover error) from the previous stage using its own codebook; summing the selected code vectors from all stages reconstructs the input, giving high accuracy at a low bit rate. It is a core component of neural audio codecs such as SoundStream and EnCodec.
fields.plain_english: A way to shrink audio into very little data by rounding it off in a few passes. Each pass fixes the small error left by the one before. It is like guessing a price in rounds: first the tens, then the ones, then the cents.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to represent audio or other signals with very few bits while keeping quality high, by splitting the job across several small codebooks instead of one huge one.
fields.practical_application: An engineer working with modern AI audio or low-bitrate speech tools meets RVQ as the layer that turns audio into the compact tokens those systems store and transmit.
common_mistakes: Confusing this with dynamic-range compression; it is data quantization, not audio level control.
Assuming one big codebook is used, when RVQ deliberately chains several small ones.
Thinking each stage re-encodes the whole signal, rather than only the leftover error from the stage before.
scenario_contexts: Understanding how a neural audio codec turns sound into discrete tokens.
Trading bit rate against audio quality by choosing the number of quantizer stages.
Reading the technical docs of an AI music or speech model that lists an RVQ bottleneck.

sources: Zeghidour et al., SoundStream: An End-to-End Neural Audio Codec, IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech and Language Processing (2021), DOI 10.1109/TASLP.2021.3129994
Gray, Vector Quantization, IEEE ASSP Magazine (1984)

fields.definition: Riffusion is an AI music-generation system, released in 2022 by Seth Forsgren and Hayk Martiros, that fine-tunes the Stable Diffusion image model to generate spectrogram images from text prompts and then converts those spectrograms back into audio.
fields.plain_english: Riffusion makes music from text by drawing a picture of the sound and turning that picture into audio. It reuses an image AI to do it.
fields.purpose_function: It repurposes a text-to-image diffusion model for music by treating sound as spectrogram images, showing that existing image models can generate short musical clips from text descriptions.
fields.practical_application: A user types a style prompt into Riffusion, which generates a spectrogram and renders a short audio clip, useful for quick musical sketches or experimentation.
common_mistakes: Thinking Riffusion generates audio directly - it generates spectrogram images that are then converted to sound
Expecting long, structured songs rather than short clips
Assuming spectrogram-to-audio conversion is lossless
scenario_contexts: Generating a short musical riff from a text prompt
Experimenting with spectrogram-based music generation
Creating novelty clips by blending style prompts

sources: Riffusion official documentation (riffusion.com) and reference implementation (github.com/riffusion/riffusion-hobby)
Rombach et al., High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models (Stable Diffusion, 2022)

flags: All fields left blank: 'rubbery' is a subjective, informal timbre descriptor with no authoritative or standardized definition. A literature search (professional synthesis texts, manufacturer docs, standards) returned no acceptable source defining it; only forums, blogs, and videos use the term, none of which count. Unlike 'squelchy' (attested by Roland and tied to a specific resonant-filter mechanism), 'rubbery' maps to no single agreed technique, so it is left unauthored pending an authoritative source.

fields.definition: A circuit or module that captures (samples) the instantaneous value of an input signal at moments set by a clock or trigger and holds that value steady at its output until the next sample. In synthesizers it is most often fed with noise to generate stepped random voltages for modulation; in data conversion it is the front-end stage that freezes an analog value while an ADC digitizes it.
fields.plain_english: It grabs the level of a signal at a chosen moment and keeps it steady until the next grab. Feeding it noise gives those classic random, stepping computer bleeps in synth music.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to turn a smoothly changing signal into a series of held steps, either to create rhythmic random modulation in synths or to hold a steady voltage so a converter can measure it accurately.
fields.practical_application: A technician patches noise into a sample-and-hold clocked by the LFO to modulate filter cutoff, adding stepped random movement to a patch.
common_mistakes: Forgetting sample-and-hold needs a clock or trigger; with no clock it just holds one value.
Assuming its output is smooth, when it is stepped and changes only at each sample.
Thinking it always makes random values, when the output depends entirely on the signal you feed it.
scenario_contexts: Creating stepped random filter modulation by feeding noise into a clocked sample-and-hold.
Understanding the sample-and-hold stage at the input of an ADC in a digital audio interface.
Clocking sample-and-hold to tempo for rhythmic random pitch or timbre changes.

sources: Sound on Sound - Synth Secrets series (LFOs, noise and modulation)
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (sample-and-hold and A/D conversion)

fields.definition: A device or software that stores and plays back a timed sequence of musical events - pitches, gates or triggers, and control values - driving synthesizers or other instruments to perform them automatically. Hardware step sequencers advance through a fixed number of steps, while MIDI and DAW sequencers record and edit note and controller data on a timeline.
fields.plain_english: A tool that remembers a pattern of notes and plays it back for you, over and over, in time. It is like a player-piano roll that tells the synth which notes to hit and when.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to automate performance so the musician does not have to play every note live, letting patterns loop, layer, and stay perfectly in time.
fields.practical_application: A technician programs a bassline into a step sequencer, sets the tempo, and clocks it so it locks with the rest of the rig.
common_mistakes: Confusing a sequencer, which stores note events, with a synthesizer, which makes the sound.
Forgetting to match clock or tempo, so the sequence drifts out of time with other gear.
Mixing up a step sequencer's steps with musical bars, leading to wrong pattern lengths.
scenario_contexts: Programming a repeating bassline or drum pattern on a hardware step sequencer.
Recording and editing MIDI notes on a DAW's piano-roll sequencer.
Slaving an external sequencer to the studio's master clock so everything stays in sync.

sources: MIDI Association - MIDI 1.0 specification (note and clock messages)
Huber & Runstein, Modern Recording Techniques (MIDI sequencing)
